2. The brief facts relevant for disposal of this Rule are that the pre-emptor-opposite party No.1 as pre-emptor filed Miscellaneous (Pre-emption) Case No. 1 of 1996 under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act before the learned Assistant Judge, Meherpur impleading the petitioners and others on the averments that the suit land situated under Police Station and District- Meherpur, Mouza-Amjhupi, B.A. Dag No. 2105, R.S. Dag No. 2913 measuring. 15 acres of land belonged to the Government and out of which 10 decimals of land was allotted to the pre-emptor-applicant and pre-emptee-opposite party No. 3 (petitioner No. 1) vide Bandobasto Case No. 18/X11/64-65; that R.S. record was prepared in their name and rest 5 decimals of land adjacent to the land of the pre-emptor and opposite party No. 3 was settled in favour of the opposite party No. 2, Md. Aftabuddin, who without serving any notice of transfer upon the pre-emptor transferred his portion of land to the pre-emptee-opposite party No. 1, wife of the opposite party No. 3 (petitioner No. 1) on 4.10.1995; that pre-emptee-opposite party No. 1 is a stranger to the case jote, the pre-emptor needs land and hence the case for pre-emption. 

 3. The pre-emptee-opposite party Nos. 1 and 3 appeared in the case and filed joint written statement denying all the material allegation of the application for pre-emption contending, inter-alia, that the pre-emptor is not a co-sharer to the case land and the pre-emptee-opposite party Nos.1 is not a stranger to the case land; that opposite party No. 3 is the co-sharer to the case land, who purchased the case land by his hard-earned money in the name of his wife Halima Begum, pre-emptee opposite party No. 1 and as such the application for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act is not maintainable. Besides the Govt. allotted plots are not subject of pre-emption. It has been also contended that the case land is a residential house and pre-emptee opposite party No.1 and opposite party No. 3 purchase the suit land within the full knowledge of the pre-emptor, who after purchase made construction over the case land but the pre-emptor by suppressing those facts filed the case for pre-emption with a malafide intention. It has been further contended that opposite party No. 2, Aftab uddin after getting settlement of the case land did not able to recover his possession because the pre-emptee and her husband (petitioner Nos. 1 and 2) are in possession for more then 30 years in the case land along with other adjacent and in such background the opposite party No. 2, Aftab uddin decided to sale the suit property to the petitioners for avoiding litigation and as such the pre-emption application is liable to be rejected. 

 10. Mr. Ehia, the learned Advocate relying on the decision namely in the case of Shah Alam (Md.) Vs. Md. Shahidur Rahman and others reported in 55 IDR 214 submits that Joma bandabasta of the land in question has been separated by R.S. Khatian No. 1852 (Ext.2) and DCR which also admitted by the pre-emptor himself as PW-1 and therefore, pre-emptor having ceased to be a co-sharer in the case land, he had no locus standi to claim pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Mr. Ehia, thereafter, referring to the entire evidence on record submits that there is nothing on record to show that the pre-emptor-opposite party is a contiguous land owner or the petitioner opposite party No. 1 Halima Begum (vendee) is a stranger to the case land but the both the Courts below upon ignoring the material evidences on record under misconception of law and facts abruptly allowed the pre-emption application resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. 

 14. In deciding the matter, I have carefully examined the material evidences on record including the dispositions of PWS and OPWs. to the best of my ability. It appears that the pre-emptor himself was examined as PW-1, who in his deposition admitted that he along with opposite party No. 3 (husband of the pre-emptee purchaser) got total 10 decimals of land by way of permanent settlement. This witness in his cross-examination stated that: 

 16. It is found that opposite party No. 3, Sukur Ali himself (petitioner No.1) was examined OPW-1, who also deposed on behalf of his wife pre-emptee-petitioner No.2, Halima Begum. This witness stated that he is a co-sharer to the case jote by way of permanent settlement, vide Bandobasto Case No. 18/XII/64-65. This witness also stated that:" 

 17. This witness next stated that: ঐ ১০ শতক জমির মধ্যে ৫ শতক জমির স্বত্ব ২ নংও, পি, দাবীকরিলে আমি গন্ডগোল এড়ানোর জন্য ২ নং ও, পি, কে ২০০০/- টাকা দিয়ে ৫ শতক জমি রেজিঃ দলিল করিয়া নেই। দলিলটি আমার ও আমার স্ত্রীর নামে হওয়ার কথা ছিল। কিন্তু আমি রেজিঃ অফিসে উপস্থিত না থাকতে শুধু আমার স্ত্রীর নামে হ���য়াছ্। পরে আমি ঐ জমি আমার স্ত্রীর নিকট হইতে আমার নামে রেজিঃ করিয়া নিয়াছি। " This wistness further stated that: "আমি বরাবর ১০ শতক জমি দখল করিয়া আসিতেছি। আমার বসবাস করা ১০ শতক জমির মধ্যে যদি নাঃ ৫ শতক জমি দরখাস্তকারী pre-emption মূলে পায় তবে আমার মারাত্বক অসুবিধা হইবে।” It is found that OPW 2, A. Sattar and OPW-3, A. Mannan both of them in their respective testimony corroborated the evidence of OPW-1 in respect of all material particulars. 

 19. On consideration of the evidence on record both oral and documentary, I do not find any logic to hold that the petitioner No. 2, Halima Begum is a stranger to the case jote. Moreover, I have already noticed that petitioner No. 1, Sukur Ali, himself as OPW-1 categorically testified that he is a contiguous owner/co-sharer of the case land and he purchased the land under pre-emption by his earned money in the name of his wife, petitioner No. 2, Helima Begum. Further, in this case pre-emptor examined in all 4 witnesses including pre-emptor himself was examined as PW-1 but on thorough scrutiny of their depositions it appears that none of the PWs deposed any single word that the pre-emptee petitioner No 2, Halima Begum (vendee) is a stranger to the case land rather PW-1, stated is his deposition that petitioner No. 1, Sukur Ali (husband of petitioner No. 2 Halima Begum) is a co-sharer to the case land. The Courts below therefore were absolutely wrong in holding that the pre-emptee (purchaser) Halima Begum is out and out stranger to the case land. Therefore, I am unable to accept the submissions of Mr. Md. Ruhul Amin Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor opposite party. 

 21. It is contended that Joma has been separated by R.S. Khatian No. 1852 (Ext. 2) which also admitted by the pre-emptor himself as PW-1 in which pre-emptor having cased to be a co-sharer in the case land, he had no locus standi to claim pre-emption under section 96 of the Sate Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 22. In reply Mr. Ruhul Amin Bhuiyan, the learned Advocate for the pre-emptor opposite party submits that in an application for pre-emption under section 96 of the Sate Acquisition and Tenancy Act this contention is misconceived. To resolve this point I have carefully examined the materials on record and it seems to me the land in question being non-agricultural in nature. Since it is found joma of the pre-emptor is split up by opening a new khatian No. 1852 (Ext.2), the pre-emptor can not be held to be a co-shearer to the case land and in that view of the matter also the pre-emptor is not entitled to pre-emption. 

 23. The clear legislative intent in section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act to shut the door against all the strangers who shall encroach upon the ownership and possession of the real co-sharers and whereupon, the real co-sharers can remain in enjoyment of their property and others cannot interfere with their right and possession. In this case, I have already indicated that there are sufficient evidences on record to show that petitioner No. 1, Sukur Ali (husband of petitioner No. 2 Halima Begum) is a co-sharer as well as contiguous owner of the case land purchased the case land by his own money in the name of his wife petitioner No. 2 Halima Begum and none of the PWs deposed that petitioner No.2 Halima Begum is a stranger to the case land. The concurrent findings of both Courts below that the pre-emptee purchaser Halima Begum is out and out stranger to the case land which are in fact, based on misinterpretation of laws and also contrary to the weight of evidence on record. Therefore, I find there is a good deal of substance in the contention raised by Mr. Md. Ehia, that the trial Court as well as the appellate Court below failed to decide the vital aspect of this case that who is the stranger and who is not which resulted in the failure of justice.
